previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis and a history of failed kidney transplant presented with a pruritic rash affecting his hands, feet, and eyes, which began hours after receiving cefazolin during a thrombolytic procedure for a dialysis fistula clot. Evaluation revealed no signs of infection or fistula complications. The rash and symptoms were attributed to an allergic reaction to cefazolin, supported by his documented allergy and improvement with diphenhydramine and artificial tears. Blood tests confirmed eosinophilia, a long-standing finding previously evaluated and deemed of unknown origin. A chest X-ray showed stable, slowly progressive micronodular interstitial disease, likely hypersensitivity pneumonia, with no acute infection. The patient responded well to treatment, completed inpatient hemodialysis, and was discharged home with instructions to avoid cefazolin, use short-term antihistamines and eye drops, and follow up with his primary care provider regarding eosinophilia.

Brief Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted ___ with fevers, chills, and 
an itching confluent full-body rash that started after he was 
given cefazolin at dialysis on ___ for what was presumed to 
be an infection of his dialysis catheter (purulent drainage had 
been expressed per the dialysis note). On admission, suspicion 
for a line infection was low given normal vital signs, clean 
line/peripheral blood cultures, and lack of expressed drainage 
from the ___ site, so antibiotics were stopped. On ___, the 
patient was also complaining of knee pain. A knee effusion with 
overlying erythema was present and the fluid was tapped. Cell 
count was normal and the culture and gram stain were negative. 
This was presumed to be a reactive arthritis in the setting of 
systemic allergic reaction, rather than gout flare. Knee films 
were ordered. On ___ the patient went to normally scheduled 
dialysis and during treatment began to have eruption of new 
erythematous, itching patches over the left brow, abdomen and 
left hand. There was also left-hand swelling. He was given 
hydrocortisone IV, famotidine IV and Benadryl and the rash and 
swelling improved.  On ___, he was started on prednisone, which 
led to improvement of his knee pain. Knee films were negative 
for fracture or chrondrocalcinosis. A dermatology consult was 
obtained regarding the rashes, which were considered to most 
likely represent a fixed drug reaction. The patient was 
prescribed topical clobetasole for the rashes and on ___ was 
ready for discharge. Urine culture returned presumptive ___ 
proteus but given that the patient is asymptomatic, the 
urinalysis on that same sample does not imply infection, and he 
has poor urine output at baseline, Renal was inclined not to 
treat and consider this colonization.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,
You were admitted on ___ with fevers, chills, and an 
itchy rash that started after you were given the antibiotic 
cefazolin at dialysis on ___ for what was presumed to be an 
infection of your dialysis catheter. During your admission, we 
were not convinced there was an infection, so antibiotics were 
stopped. You also complained of knee pain and we took fluid from 
the right knee which did not appear to be gout or a joint 
infection. You had dialysis on ___ during which your felt 
your rash was worse and you had left arm swelling. We treated 
you with hydrocortisone, famotidine and Benadryl and the rash 
and swelling improved.  Your knee pain responded to prednisone. 
You were seen by dermatology about your rash and they gave 
recommendations to use clobetasole cream for two weeks. 

We have made the following changes to your home medications:
1. Started prednisone 20 mg a day. Take for 5 days after 
discharge.
2. Increased sevelamer from 3200 mg a day to 4000 mg.
3. Started Benadryl as needed for itching.
4. Started topical clobetasole ointment to apply to the rash 
areas twice a day for two weeks. 

Weigh yourself every morning, call MD if weight goes up more 
than 3 lbs.
